testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Results of 303 patents-in-fee at Shoshone Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 patents issued 1907-1930 covering average 80-acre allotments of good irrigable agricultural land. Blood quantum breakdown: 1 full-blood, 3 three-fourths, 2 five-eighths, 5 one-half, 2 three-eighths, 3 one-fourth, 7 five-sixteenths, 9 one-eighth, and others. About 90% sold or mortgaged lands. Few made beneficial use of proceeds for livestock and agricultural equipment; majority squandered in extravagant living and automobiles. Recommended holding back at least 160 acres. Reservation not adapted for farming. Recommended great caution in granting patents to females as husbands squander property, desertions frequent, women left with children. Those who went broke and settled down to work for wages made better showing than on allotments. Reservation environments are the great drawback.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Effects of patents-in-fee at Cheyenne & Arapaho Agency
testimony.key_claims: In practically every case lands have been sold. Many used money unwisely but possibly a majority used proceeds for some benefit - improvement of other lands or investment in business. On the whole believes it has been beneficial to give able-bodied competent Indians their patents. Agency officials do not follow up Indian activities after patent issued. Indians resent follow-up efforts. Recommended examining each individual case as to age, opportunity and physical capacity. If mentally and physically competent, favored turning them loose. Indians are no different than any other race regarding extravagance.

testimony.witness_title: United States Indian Farmer, Yankton Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Views on releasing Santee and Yankton Sioux from supervision
testimony.key_claims: As long as Indian's land held in trust he will never take his place in affairs of life among white brothers. Every young able-bodied Indian whose mind is functioning properly should have everything turned over unrestricted. Opposes reserving part of allotment as compromise. Indian should be either full citizen or ward. Does not know a single Santee Indian who received patent to entire allotment and still owns all of it. Among Yankton Sioux a few cases of patentees who still own all land and built good homes. Most disposed of land and used money in riotous living. Sooner they are broke and have to work the better. Identified Joseph Ellis and Thomas Hunter of Lake Andes as doing well; Simon Vasser and Gilbert St. Pierre among those who sold.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Detailed report on patents-in-fee at Yankton Sioux reservation
testimony.key_claims: 599 patents to entire allotments and 13 for portions issued. Not more than 10 own entire original allotments; not more than 50 own any portion. Practically 550 disposed of all land; about 400 have absolutely nothing to show. Originally 3113 allotments comprising 368,400 acres; today not exceeding 59,000 acres held in trust. Allotments varied 80-320 acres. Mixed-bloods obtained twice the land through sharp practice of having agricultural land classified as grazing. Indians typically sell immediately after patent; within 12 months have nothing. Principal squandering through automobile purchases and joy-riding. White men beset Indians upon patent receipt to buy land at inadequate prices. About 60% of able-bodied members farming to some extent. Believes in issuing patents to entire allotments rather than partial. One of great mistakes is leaving impression that US is still responsible after release. Transitory period of suffering is necessary.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee effects and competency policy at Rosebud Agency
testimony.key_claims: More than 17,000 Indians received patents since 1917 nationally. Opposes granting patents 'in the bulk.' Each case should be decided on own merits irrespective of blood status or educational qualifications. Approximately 600 of allotments under agency received patents. About 90% immediately sold or mortgaged lands. 85% of tracts were 160 acres, valued $1000-$16000, average $4000 per quarter. Not one in ten Indians purchases teams, farm implements, or makes improvements. An Indian capable of earning living may still be classified as competent even if he wastes property proceeds. Recommends Office outline standard for competency commissioners and superintendents.
